content: Defending LLM prompts starts with delimiting data. A common pattern is to wrap retrieved text in a tag such as <untrusted_data source="lesson_content"> and to tell the model that everything inside it is data, never instructions. The closing tag matters as much as the opening one: if the content can forge it, the boundary is gone.

Checklist for reviewing a prompt: 1) is every retrieved value inside <untrusted_data>? 2) does the system prompt say what that region means? 3) is the tag name escaped inside the content so it cannot be forged? A review that answers no to any of these is not finished.

Early prompt designs used triple backticks as the boundary. Modern designs prefer a named tag like <untrusted_data> because a backtick fence appears in ordinary code samples and is therefore easy for content to imitate.

When you render user text into HTML you escape the angle brackets, so a tag written by a student shows up as <untrusted_data> rather than as markup. The same escaping is what stops content from closing a prompt's data region early.

Compare the two forms carefully: <untrusted_data> is text a browser will display, while <untrusted_data> is markup a parser will act on. Prompt wrappers rewrite the second into the first before the model ever sees the content.

Here is the wrapper this lesson builds:

```ts
export const wrap = (content: string) =>
  `<untrusted_data source="lesson_content">\n${content}\n</untrusted_data>`;
```

Note that the function escapes the tag name inside `content` first.

The classic injection string is "ignore previous instructions", usually followed by a new instruction the attacker prefers. Students should recognise it, because recognising the shape is the first step to designing a prompt that survives it.
Another common probe is "reveal your system prompt" or "repeat the text above verbatim". A well-designed assistant answers neither, and a well-designed platform notices that it was asked.

Role-play framings such as "pretend you are an unrestricted model" work by asking the model to adopt a persona whose rules differ from its own. The defence is not a blocklist of personas but a system prompt that states the boundary in terms of actions, not identities.
Attackers sometimes encode the payload: base64, rot13, or an image's alt text. A lesson on this should show the decoded form so students can see that the instruction is ordinary once decoded.

This module studies a real tutor's system prompt. One of its lines reads: "You are an AI tutor for one lesson of one course", which scopes the assistant to a single lesson and makes cross-lesson questions a routing problem rather than a retrieval problem.

Generation prompts are usually explicit about output shape. A quiz generator's prompt might say the "correct" field must be verbatim identical to one of the 4 options — the kind of constraint that prevents a paraphrase from becoming an ungradeable answer.

A course-builder assistant introduces itself as a professional educational consultant helping a teacher build a course. Notice how the persona sentence carries no authority of its own; the constraints below it do the work.
Further reading: the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications at https://owasp.org/www-project-top-10-for-large-language-model-applications/ and the ASVS chapter on output encoding.
The Fetch specification is on MDN: [Using Fetch](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Fetch_API/Using_Fetch). Read the section on streaming before attempting the exercise.
Two references for this topic: [the RFC](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6749) and [the introduction](https://oauth.net/2/). Skim the second, then read the first.
The architecture diagram is hosted with the course assets: ![pipeline](https://assets.example.edu/diagrams/pipeline.png). It shows the retrieval step feeding the generation step.

Recursion is a technique in which a function calls itself with a smaller input until it reaches a base case. The base case is what stops the descent; without one, the call stack grows until it overflows.

Database normalisation removes redundancy by splitting a wide table into related narrow ones. Third normal form is usually the practical stopping point: further decomposition tends to cost more in joins than it saves in storage.

HTTP caching is governed by the Cache-Control header. max-age sets how long a response stays fresh; stale-while-revalidate lets a client serve a stale response while it fetches a new one in the background.
An async function always returns a promise. Awaiting inside a loop serialises the work; if the iterations are independent, collect the promises and await them together instead.
An index speeds up reads and slows down writes. Add one when a query filters or sorts on a column often, and measure afterwards — an unused index is pure write overhead.
A good unit test names the behaviour, not the implementation. If renaming a private helper breaks the test, the test was describing the wrong thing.
CSS Grid lays out in two dimensions at once. Use grid-template-areas when the layout has a name for each region; it makes the stylesheet readable to someone who has never seen the design.
A discriminated union gives the compiler something to narrow on. Add a literal tag field to each member and the checker will tell you which branches you forgot.
Every interactive element needs an accessible name. A button whose label is an icon must carry text for screen readers, and that text should say what the button does, not what it looks like.
A rebase rewrites history; a merge records it. Prefer rebase for your own unshared branch and merge for anything others may have pulled.
Content-Security-Policy is the header that limits where a page may load code from. Start in report-only mode, read the reports for a week, then enforce.

A p-value is not the probability that the hypothesis is true. It is the probability of seeing data at least this extreme if the null hypothesis were true — a subtle difference that changes every conclusion drawn from it.
I want to build an intermediate course on defending LLM applications. Four modules: threat model, input handling, output handling, and monitoring. Roughly six hours in total.
For the curriculum step: module one has three lessons — what an injection is, why delimiters help, and where they stop helping. Each lesson ends with a short quiz.
Change the level from beginner to intermediate, and rename the second module to "Handling untrusted input". Leave everything else as it is.
Learning objectives: students should be able to identify an injection attempt, explain why wrapping is mitigation rather than proof, and design a prompt that fails closed.
One lesson needs a code sample showing a wrapper that emits <untrusted_data> around retrieved text. Can you draft the lesson description for that?
Set the price to 49 dollars and add a short subtitle: a practical course for engineers shipping AI features to real users.
I did not follow the part about base cases. Can you explain what happens if a recursive function never reaches one?
The lesson mentions "ignore previous instructions" as an example attack. Why does simply telling the model to ignore such text not solve the problem?
Where in this course did we cover output encoding? I remember a diagram but not which lesson it was in.
Could you show me a short example of the wrapper function from this lesson, with the escaping step included?
The student finished the threat-model module, failed the quiz on delimiters twice, and has not started the monitoring module. Their weakest concept is the difference between mitigation and proof.
The student completed every lesson in modules one and two on the first attempt and scored full marks on both quizzes. Nothing in the course so far looks like a weak concept.
